title: Analysis: China’s CO2 emissions fall in Q2 2026 due to plummeting oil use - Carbon Brief
gist: China's CO2 emissions fell 1% in Q2 2026 for the first time ever driven by collapsing oil use rather than coal, as the Strait of Hormuz crisis accelerated an already-underway EV-driven structural shift in transport, even as coal power kept rising because of worsening wind/solar curtailment and a new wave of coal-plant construction; China's new five-year plans quietly soften prior coal-reduction ambitions while loosening curtailment limits.

themes.theme: Headline emissions trend: oil, not coal, drives the fall

insights.claim: China's CO2 emissions fell 1% in Q2 2026 as oil use plunged amid the Strait of Hormuz crisis — the first time on record that a fall in oil consumption alone was sufficient to drive an overall decline in China's emissions, whereas coal consumption had always been the deciding factor in every previous case.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Signals a structural change in what drives China's emissions trajectory — investors tracking China climate policy should now weight oil/transport dynamics, not just coal, as a swing factor.
insights.quote: This is the first time that reductions in oil consumption have been responsible for a fall in CO2 emissions overall – in all previous cases, coal consumption has been the main driver.
insights.locator: Opening summary

insights.claim: China's oil use fell 9% overall and 16% for the transport sector specifically in Q2 2026, following disruptions to Gulf oil supply through the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of China's transport-fuel demand shock, a leading indicator for global oil demand and refining-margin forecasts.
insights.locator: Opening summary

insights.claim: China's total CO2 emissions from fossil fuels and cement have plateaued for more than two years since peaking in March 2024; after a 2% year-on-year rise in Q1 2026, the 1% Q2 decline leaves H1 2026 emissions only marginally higher than a year earlier and still below the 2023-24 peak.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Establishes the multi-year plateau as the baseline against which any renewed decline should be judged — China has not yet convincingly broken below its 2023-24 emissions peak.
insights.locator: Emissions still flat

insights.claim: The author frames China's ongoing emissions trajectory as 'a race between energy demand growth and clean-energy growth,' noting both have slowed this year, meaning the net emissions direction depends on which side decelerates faster.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: A useful mental model for forecasting China's emissions path quarter to quarter: watch relative deceleration of demand versus clean-capacity additions rather than absolute levels alone.
insights.quote: The emission trend remains a race between energy demand growth and clean-energy growth, both of which have slowed down this year.
insights.locator: Opening summary

insights.claim: Given structural pressure on oil demand, continued declines in real-estate construction, and slower coal-chemicals growth, the author expects China's full-year 2026 CO2 emissions could still fall.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: A directional full-year emissions call investors and policy trackers can use as a benchmark to test against Q3/Q4 data releases.
insights.locator: Opening summary

themes.theme: The Hormuz oil shock and how much was real demand destruction

insights.claim: China cut crude oil imports by 32% in Q2 2026, with crude processing volumes down 11% and Sinopec sales down 9%, but roughly 60% of the import decline was covered by drawing down China's oil stockpiles rather than by genuine consumption cuts.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Important nuance for oil-market analysts: the headline 32% import collapse overstates real Chinese demand destruction — a large share is a one-off inventory drawdown that could reverse and pull imports back up later.
insights.locator: Oil use plummeted while coal grew

insights.claim: National Bureau of Statistics energy-mix data show China's actual oil consumption fell about 3% in H1 2026 and around 9% in Q2 alone, confirming that genuine demand reduction — not just inventory drawdown — played a substantial role.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Gives a cleaner, inventory-adjusted read on the true pace of Chinese oil-demand decline for modeling global crude balances.
insights.locator: Oil use plummeted while coal grew

insights.claim: China's plunging oil imports during the Hormuz crisis have been 'widely hailed as the most important price stabilising factor for the global oil market.'
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Directly ties Chinese domestic demand destruction to global crude price stability during a Gulf supply crisis — a macro linkage relevant to oil-price and geopolitical-risk positioning.
insights.quote: The dramatic fall in China’s demand for oil imports during the Hormuz crisis has been widely hailed as the most important price stabilising factor for the global oil market.
insights.locator: What drove the fall in oil consumption?

insights.claim: Sinopec had already forecast 6% and 5% declines in diesel and petrol consumption for 2026 before the war on Iran began; actual H1 2026 sales fell 9%, indicating the Hormuz crisis accelerated a pre-existing structural demand decline rather than causing it outright.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Contrarian correction to narratives crediting the geopolitical crisis alone: the oil-demand decline was already underway from EV substitution before the crisis hit, meaning the trend is more durable than a crisis-driven spike would be.
insights.locator: What drove the fall in oil consumption?

insights.claim: Chinese transport activity was stable-to-growing overall in Q2 2026 (cross-regional passenger trips +0.1% YoY, urban trips +2.9%, commercial freight tonnage +2.4%), except for air travel, where passenger numbers fell 7% in May-June after 7% growth in Q1 — showing the oil-demand drop reflects a fuel-source shift, not a mobility collapse.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Rules out the alternative explanation that Chinese oil demand fell because people simply traveled less — the substitution is toward electricity, which is a structurally different (and more durable) story than a recession-driven demand drop.
insights.locator: What drove the fall in oil consumption?

themes.theme: EVs as a structural force displacing oil

insights.claim: Oil consumption displaced by EVs in China in H1 2026 exceeded the UK's total oil consumption over the same six-month period.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: A vivid scale comparison showing China's EV fleet now displaces oil demand equivalent to a mid-sized developed economy's entire consumption — a material factor in global oil-demand forecasts.
insights.locator: What drove the fall in oil consumption?

insights.claim: The oil-displacement effect of EVs was almost twice as large as would be expected purely from the growth in the number of EVs on the road, because the usage (utilization) of existing EVs also surged.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Key nuance: EV oil displacement is being driven by both fleet growth and rising per-vehicle usage, meaning oil-demand models based on EV sales/stock alone will understate the true displacement effect.
insights.quote: The effect of EVs on oil consumption was almost twice as large as would be expected based on the increase in the number of EVs on the road alone, as the usage of existing EVs surged.
insights.locator: Key findings

insights.claim: EVs avoided an estimated 19 million tonnes of oil equivalent (Mtoe) of consumption in Q2 2026 alone, up 50% year-on-year, bringing total EV-displaced oil to 36 Mtoe for H1 2026 — equal to about 4.5% of China's 2025 oil imports over the same period.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Concrete, rapidly-growing displacement volume useful for calibrating global oil-demand-growth forecasts that account for Chinese electrification.
insights.locator: What drove the fall in oil consumption?

insights.claim: If EV sales and charging growth continue at H1 2026 rates through the second half of the year, EV-driven oil displacement could reach about 80 million tonnes for full-year 2026 — roughly equal to Mexico's total oil consumption.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Gives a forward-looking full-year magnitude for China's EV-driven oil displacement, a testable benchmark for 2026 year-end data.
insights.locator: What drove the fall in oil consumption?

insights.claim: Estimated CO2 emissions avoided through EV adoption were about 35 MtCO2 in Q2 2026 — equal to 1.3% of China's total quarterly emissions — after netting out the power-sector emissions generated to charge those vehicles.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Quantifies EVs' direct emissions-avoidance contribution net of grid carbon intensity, useful for assessing the real climate payoff of China's EV transition given its still coal-heavy grid.
insights.locator: What drove the fall in oil consumption?

insights.claim: Despite rapid growth, the year-on-year increase in EV-displaced oil accounts for only about a third of the total drop in China's H1 2026 oil consumption, and that consumption drop itself explains only about half of the drop in oil imports — the remainder comes from inventory drawdown, slower chemicals-industry growth, and behavioral/operational adaptation.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: A disciplined corrective against overstating EVs' role in the current oil-demand story — most of the import collapse is temporary (stockpile drawdown), so a rebound in imports is plausible even as the EV trend itself continues.
insights.locator: What drove the fall in oil consumption?

insights.claim: Electric heavy-truck sales rose about 77% year-on-year in Q2 2026 (June sales more than doubled), with electric trucks exceeding 45% market share of new truck sales, making trucks the fastest-growing source of oil displacement — avoided fuel use from trucks was up 90% year-on-year in H1 2026.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Heavy-truck electrification is now outpacing passenger EV growth as an oil-displacement driver — a segment worth tracking closely for diesel-demand and battery/commercial-EV supply-chain investment theses.
insights.locator: What drove the fall in oil consumption?

insights.claim: EV charging volumes rose 60% in Q2 2026, far outpacing the 33% year-on-year growth in the on-road EV fleet, implying existing EVs (including plug-in hybrids) are being used more intensively, helped by intense price competition pushing down electric-taxi fares just as private petrol-vehicle costs rose.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Signals a second wave of oil displacement beyond fleet growth — utilization intensity — that could keep accelerating oil-demand erosion even if EV sales growth itself slows.
insights.locator: What drove the fall in oil consumption?

themes.theme: Coal power's stubborn rebound and the curtailment problem

insights.claim: China's power-sector emissions rose 3.0% in H1 2026 (reversing a 3.2% decline in H1 2025), despite 9% higher hydro output, growing nuclear generation, record wind/solar capacity additions, and slowing power-demand growth (down from 5.9% to 5.2% year-on-year) — the cause was a rise in curtailed ('wasted') solar and wind generation plus exceptionally poor wind conditions.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: The central structural finding of the piece: China's renewable buildout is outpacing its grid's ability to absorb it, so capacity growth alone will not translate into falling power-sector emissions until curtailment is fixed.
insights.locator: Coal power continued to rise despite clean-capacity growth

insights.claim: Absent the rise in renewable curtailment and the unusually poor wind year, coal-fired power generation and power-sector emissions would also have fallen in 2026.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: A counterfactual that isolates curtailment (a fixable market-design problem) as the specific lever that would flip power-sector emissions from rising to falling.
insights.locator: Coal power continued to rise despite clean-capacity growth

insights.claim: The structural cause of curtailment is that China's power-grid dispatch model and electricity market neither require nor reward flexible operation of coal and hydro plants or inter-provincial transmission lines — generator prices and transmission volumes are fixed months in advance, and coal plants earn 'capacity payments' for being available rather than for adjusting output to conditions.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Identifies market-design reform (not just more storage or transmission) as the root fix needed for China to absorb its renewable buildout — a key policy variable to watch in future five-year-plan implementation.
insights.locator: Coal power continued to rise despite clean-capacity growth

insights.claim: New coal-power capacity additions reached 30GW in H1 2026 — the highest half-year level since 2016 — with a further 25GW starting construction and less than 3GW retired, meaning the ongoing coal buildout itself is limiting how much new wind and solar can displace existing coal generation.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: China is still adding large amounts of new coal capacity even as it builds renewables, creating a structural overhang that will keep coal generation elevated for years regardless of renewable growth rates.
insights.locator: Coal power continued to rise despite clean-capacity growth

insights.claim: China's new five-year plan raises the allowed curtailment ceiling to as high as 15% in resource-rich provinces (up from a 2024-set 10%, itself raised from an original 5%), even though reported national curtailment already implies a rate below the plan's 'around 10%' target — meaning the new limits are looser than recent real-world performance rather than tightening standards.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: A policy detail that undercuts the headline narrative of stronger renewable-integration ambition — investors should read new curtailment targets skeptically rather than assume tightening.
insights.locator: Outlook for China's CO2 emissions

insights.claim: Monthly curtailment data has stopped being published in China recently, and reported curtailment figures have historically understated actual curtailment 'by a wide margin,' raising the possibility that the indicator itself is being revised or its transparency reduced.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: A data-transparency red flag: disappearing curtailment statistics make it harder for outside analysts to verify whether China's renewable-integration problem is improving or worsening — worth monitoring for reporting changes.
insights.quote: Reported data has understated actual curtailment by a wide margin, compared to implied curtailment.
insights.locator: Outlook for China's CO2 emissions

insights.claim: Battery storage capacity grew by 17GW in H1 2026, bringing total installed capacity to 153GW, but this is a slowdown from the 23GW added in H1 2025 — even as storage is positioned as a key fix for curtailment.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Storage deployment is decelerating exactly when it's needed most to absorb rising renewable curtailment, a potential bottleneck for grid-integration equipment and battery-storage investment theses.
insights.locator: Coal power continued to rise despite clean-capacity growth

themes.theme: Other industrial sectors: chemicals, cement, steel

insights.claim: Growth in coal use for chemicals production slowed sharply to 8% in Q2 2026 (from 15% in 2025 and 19% in Q1 2026), defying expectations of a boom, because coal-processing capacity utilization was already near its ceiling — leaving no headroom to expand output even though higher oil prices made coal-based chemicals more profitable.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: A 'profitable but capacity-constrained' dynamic: rising oil prices favor coal-chemicals economically, but existing capacity limits mean this won't translate into proportionally higher coal demand until new capacity is built.
insights.locator: Oil use plummeted while coal grew

insights.claim: Cement production fell as construction volumes contracted at an accelerating pace (a 9% decline in Q2 2026 versus 8% in Q1), while crude steel output fell 1% and pig-iron production fell 3% in Q2 2026.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Confirms continued weakness in China's construction-linked heavy industry, relevant to global steel, cement and iron-ore demand forecasts.
insights.locator: Oil use plummeted while coal grew

insights.claim: Oil-based chemical production kept growing even as coal-based chemicals growth stalled — ethylene output rose 17% while primary plastics production stayed flat — indicating the chemicals sector's feedstock mix tilted toward oil.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: A feedstock-mix shift relevant to petrochemical and coal-chemical capex allocation decisions within China's chemicals industry.
insights.locator: Oil use plummeted while coal grew

insights.claim: China approved eight new nuclear reactors in July 2026, with five reactors totaling 4.5GW — including the Linglong One small modular reactor, China's second commercial SMR — expected to enter commercial operation this year; reactor commissioning is set to accelerate further given roughly 10 new reactor approvals annually since 2022.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: A steady pipeline of ~10 reactor approvals per year since 2022 signals a multi-year acceleration in nuclear commissioning ahead, relevant for nuclear supply-chain and uranium-demand forecasting.
insights.locator: Coal power continued to rise despite clean-capacity growth

insights.claim: China remains on track to add enough non-fossil generating capacity (wind, solar, nuclear, hydro) in 2026 to cover electricity demand growth of up to 5%, despite a marked slowdown in new solar capacity additions.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Suggests China's clean-capacity growth can still keep pace with electricity demand even with softer solar additions, a relevant benchmark for whether power-sector emissions can eventually turn down.
insights.locator: Opening summary

insights.claim: Wind-power capacity additions in 2026 comfortably exceed every year except record-setting 2025, while solar additions have slowed sharply — even falling behind 2024's pace, though still roughly matching 2023 levels, when more than 200GW was added by year-end.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Flags a notable divergence between wind (still near-record) and solar (clearly decelerating) capacity growth, relevant for differentiating solar- versus wind-equipment demand forecasts.
insights.locator: Coal power continued to rise despite clean-capacity growth

themes.theme: Five-year plans quietly soften coal ambition

insights.claim: China's new 2026-30 five-year plans water down Xi Jinping's 2021 pledge to 'gradually reduce coal consumption' during this period, replacing it with a target for coal consumption merely to 'enter a plateau' — a substantive retreat in stated climate ambition.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: A key, easily-missed policy downgrade: China's own long-term coal target has been quietly weakened, which should temper expectations for near-term structural coal declines despite renewable buildout headlines.
insights.quote: gradually reduce coal consumption during the 15th five-year period
insights.locator: Outlook for China's CO2 emissions

insights.claim: The new plans nonetheless set a 'higher bar' for approving new coal-power projects and, for the first time, target controlling 'coal-power generation' itself rather than just 'generation growth' — though 204GW of coal capacity still under construction complicates enforcing this 'reasonable control.'
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: The scale of coal capacity already under construction (204GW) means even tighter approval standards will take years to show up as lower coal-generation growth.
insights.locator: Outlook for China's CO2 emissions

insights.claim: The renewable-energy five-year plan broadens the definition of grid 'system reliability' to include storage, flexible demand, EVs and 'virtual power plants,' reducing coal's previously entrenched framing as the only credible source of grid reliability.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: A conceptual policy shift that could, over time, erode the standard justification used to approve new coal capacity for 'reliability' reasons.
insights.locator: Outlook for China's CO2 emissions

insights.claim: China's electrification target calls for electricity to reach 35% of energy end-use by 2030 (up from 30% in 2025) — a faster pace of increase than the prior five years (26.5% in 2020 to 30% in 2025) — with EVs targeted to reach 30% of the vehicle fleet by 2030 (up from 12% in 2025) and 25% of commercial vehicles.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: A concrete, accelerating electrification target trajectory that underpins the EV/oil-displacement thesis for the rest of the decade.
insights.locator: Outlook for China's CO2 emissions

insights.claim: The author argues the structural shift toward transport electrification is 'unlikely to be reversed,' and that faster transport electrification lowers China's oil-demand outlook while channeling more of the country's clean-energy growth toward displacing oil rather than merely competing with power-sector coal.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: A durable, high-conviction structural call: China's oil-demand decline from EVs should be treated as a persistent trend rather than a crisis-driven blip, relevant to long-term global oil-demand forecasts.
insights.quote: This trend is unlikely to be reversed.
insights.locator: Outlook for China's CO2 emissions

insights.claim: If China's total energy-demand growth continues slowing faster than its electricity-demand growth, it becomes more feasible for clean power generation to cover all incremental demand and start driving down total fossil-fuel consumption — implying a path where China's total CO2 emissions fall even while power-sector emissions merely plateau.
insights.speaker: Lauri Myllyvirta
insights.so_what: Outlines the specific macro condition (energy demand deceleration outpacing electricity demand deceleration) that would need to hold for China's total emissions to enter a durable decline — a concrete variable to track in coming quarters.
insights.locator: Coal power continued to rise despite clean-capacity growth
